Anthropic
Anthropic is the organization that launched the MCP (Model Context Protocol) open-source protocol in November 2024.

Dify
Dify is a low-code AI application development platform designed for building, testing, and deploying conversational AI workflows and agent-based applications. It features a visual workflow editor with nodes, configuration panels, and preview capabilities, enabling users to configure agent workflows, manage tool-call recursion depth, and test model tool-calling capabilities. Dify is widely used as a large model interaction framework, including in the Sanic-Web project and for the General Q&A capability, and it supports testing small models' ability to invoke MCP services.

A central aspect of Dify is its integration with the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Starting from version v1.6.0, Dify supports two-way MCP, allowing users to call any MCP server or publish their own. Dify apps can be exposed as MCP servers for any client to invoke, and the platform can quickly integrate local MCP services. It is frequently referenced in the context of connecting to MCPHub and invoking MCP tools, though multiple accounts note that this connection is unstable, with usage depending on specific methods such as SSE or MCP and analyzable through logs. In some cases, users connected Dify to MCPHub but were unable to invoke MCP tools. Dify is also referenced in testing scenarios under the section path "Imagine if > Dify测试," related to model tool calls and MCP service integration.

Dify additionally supports a plugin system, including offline plugin installation for multi-platform, multi-architecture, and cross-architecture deployments, making it suitable for pure intranet and restricted network environments. It provides configuration options for signature verification and allows installation of plugins not listed on the Dify Marketplace, which carries associated security risks. Overall, Dify serves as a versatile platform for AI workflow development, MCP service integration, and plugin management.

MCP
MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is an open-source protocol launched by Anthropic in November 2024. Its primary purpose is to standardize the integration of large language models (LLMs) with various external tools, resources, and prompts. The protocol defines how clients interact with servers to list and call these tools, resources, and prompts, typically via JSON-RPC 2.0 messages. This allows agents and workflows to natively connect and invoke tools and applications without the need for custom glue code.

MCP is designed to be a versatile and collaborative mechanism. It supports multi-model and multi-agent interactions within AI assistants and can be used to provide services and tools, such as chart generation, to language models. For instance, it works with systems like GPT-Vis to enable large models to produce visualizations from a single sentence. The protocol is also integral to platforms like Dify, where it serves as a service configuration that provides tools and resources to Agent nodes and allows resources and prompts to be used as tools. When connecting Dify to an MCPHub, MCP is one of the suggested connection methods, alongside SSE.

The implementation and deployment of MCP involve several practical considerations. It can be added locally and invoked through an MCPHub, with connection methods including SSE and MCP. It is also referenced in the context of deploying services like `antvis/mcp-server-chart`, which may require a remote service to function. A key challenge discussed is that having too many tools can cause complexity and exceed a model's context window. To address this, a proposed solution is to limit the number of MCP tools, for example, by implementing only one or two chart-generation tools so that models like Qwen3:32b can successfully invoke them. The protocol's underlying principles, its integration with large models, and troubleshooting model capability are also subjects of discussion. Furthermore, MCP is a concept that can be extended by building a local MCP platform or writing custom MCP services.

Gpt-Vis-Api
Gpt-Vis-Api is a chart generation API service that can be deployed locally or accessed as a cloud-based API. It is deployed by apconw (also referenced as the apconw/gpt-vis-api deployment) and is designed to receive JSON data requests, use AntV/G to generate various chart types—including line charts, bar charts, and organization charts—and then upload the resulting chart images to MinIO storage. After upload, the service returns pre-signed (presigned) URLs that allow frontend access to the generated images.

The service typically runs locally on port 3100, accepting POST requests at an endpoint such as http://localhost:3100/generate to produce charts and return URLs to the generated images. Its project files are located at E:\gpt-vis-api-main. Deployment involves local testing and Dify testing as part of its setup process. The service has also been described as a chart generation MCP service, and it has produced log output, for example on 2025-11-24 11:57:41, generating a JSON configuration for an organization chart.

In some usage scenarios, Gpt-Vis-Api is described as a cloud-based API that local models attempt to call, possibly represented by a cloud icon in related imagery. MCP Server
MCP Server refers to a server component or service that operates within the Model Context Protocol (MCP) ecosystem, acting as an intermediary between AI models and external tools, resources, or applications. It exchanges JSON-RPC 2.0 messages with clients, handling requests such as `tools/list`, `resources/list`, `prompts/list`, and `tools/call`. MCP servers expose tools or apps for clients to invoke and can be freely combined with open-source models. Such servers are often available through marketplaces like the ModelScope MCP marketplace.

MCP servers frequently depend on multiple runtimes such as Node.js and Python, requiring manual maintenance of numerous commands, parameters, and environment variables. A representative implementation is the FastMCP-based server defined in `mcpserver.py`, which registers weather and stock query tools and runs an HTTP service with SSE transport on host `127.0.0.1`, port `4200`, and path prefix `/demo`, with debug log level. Another variant runs with SSE transport on host `127.0.0.1`, port `4200`, path `/demo`, and debug log level. A Node.js-based MCP server runs in SSE transport mode, started with the command `node build/index.js --transport sse` from the directory `E:\mcp-server-chart-main\mcp-server-chart-main`, and handles JSON-RPC 2.0 requests from clients. Yet another instance runs on `host.docker.internal:1122`, supports `initialize` and `tools/list`, but returns "Method not found" for `resources/list`, `resources/templates/list`, and `prompts/list`. The MCP Server is also represented by the Python logo in some contexts, and is discussed as a technical topic related to the deployment and integration of services.
